# Text as Data: Tokens, Normalization, Zipf {#sec-text-as-data}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number and every code output on this page
was produced by running the code shown, with `scikit-learn` 1.9 and
`tiktoken` 0.13; the full environment is in @sec-setup. The
`LogisticRegression` results are deterministic — the default `lbfgs` solver
takes no randomness, so the `random_state` below is only an extra safeguard,
not a seed that changes anything. The tokenizer, Zipf, and vector-space explorers are
interactive.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- turn raw text into model-ready units and defend each preprocessing choice;
- explain byte-pair encoding well enough to predict how a tokenizer splits an unseen word;
- describe Zipf's law and its practical consequence, the vocabulary problem;
- derive a TF-IDF vector by hand and get the same numbers as `scikit-learn`;
- say precisely what bag-of-words can and cannot represent, and defend that in an interview;
- explain why tokenization is where multilingual pain — including Turkish morphology — begins.

## The problem, in one sentence

A model is a function that does arithmetic on numbers. A maintenance log is
a string of characters. Everything in this chapter exists to bridge that
gap, and the bridge has exactly two spans: [decide what the units are]{.hl}
(tokenization), and [decide what number each unit contributes]{.hl}
(weighting).

That is the whole chapter.

This framing is worth stating up front, because the techniques below —
bag-of-words, TF-IDF — are sometimes dismissed as historical. They are not.

The representations we build here are **sparse**: most words in the
vocabulary do not occur in any given document, so most coordinates of a
document vector stay zero. @sec-embeddings moves to **dense** vectors, which
describe each word with far fewer coordinates, most of them non-zero. Sparse
representations remain strong baselines where labels are scarce, documents are
long and topical, and literal term matching matters.

More importantly: the *decisions* they force you to make are the same
decisions a modern pipeline forces on you. Only here, you can see them.

**What we will look at.** First the units: how a string becomes tokens, why
every way of cutting it is wrong in some direction, and who pays for that in
Turkish. Then two laws about word frequencies: Zipf's, which explains why
frequencies in real text are so lopsided, and Heaps', which explains why a
growing corpus keeps showing you words you have not seen. Then the core of the
chapter — six steps that take four
short sentences all the way to vectors you can measure distances on, with
every intermediate number shown. We finish with what this representation
cannot do, which is the reason the next chapter exists.

::: {.column-margin}
A statistician's framing that will serve you for the whole chapter:
preprocessing is not preparation for the model. Preprocessing *is part of*
the model. Every choice below is a modelling assumption, and it belongs in
your methods section.
:::

## From characters to tokens {#sec-text-as-data-tokens}

::: {#gloss-tokenization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**tokenization** — cutting a run of text into the pieces the model will
count. Which pieces the model gets as separate units is not settled for you:
the structure of the language constrains the options, and the tokenizer's
design makes the call. [↩](#term-tokenization){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-token .column-margin .term-gloss}
**token** — one of those pieces. Often a word, sometimes part of a word,
sometimes a punctuation mark. When a vendor charges you "per token", this
is the thing being counted. [↩](#term-token){.term-back}
:::

Before a model can count anything, something has to decide what a *thing*
is. That decision is yours, you make it once, and everything downstream
inherits it: how large your vocabulary grows, what counts as a word the
model has never seen, and — if a vendor bills you per token — what a
sentence costs. Nobody announces this decision; it arrives disguised as a
one-line call to a library. This section is about making it on purpose.

The obvious first move is to split on whitespace. It fails immediately, and
the ways it fails are the entire design space of [tokenization](#gloss-tokenization){#term-tokenization .term-ref}.

```python
text = "The pump P-101 didn't fail; it's the seal (again!)."
print(text.split())
```

```text
['The', 'pump', 'P-101', "didn't", 'fail;', "it's", 'the', 'seal', '(again!).']
```

`fail;` and `fail` are now different [tokens](#gloss-token){#term-token .term-ref}. So are `The` and `the`. So are
`it's` and `it is`. Each of these is a decision you have to make, and each
one either merges things that should stay apart or splits things that should
stay together.

### The normalization ladder {#sec-text-as-data-normalization}

::: {#gloss-normalization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**normalization** — systematically reducing orthographic or morphological
differences you have decided do not matter for your task. Erasing case
(*Pump* → *pump*) is one kind; collapsing inflected forms onto a shared stem
or lemma (*pumps* → *pump*) is another. [↩](#term-normalization){.term-back}
:::

All of those are decisions about *erasing* differences. Which raises the
obvious question: why not erase as much as possible? Lowercase everything,
strip the punctuation, cut the words back to their stems, and your counts get
denser and your vocabulary smaller.

Because every one of those steps also destroys something, and you do not find
out what until later. Here is the standard
[normalization](#gloss-normalization){#term-normalization .term-ref} sequence, in the order people usually apply it, with the
argument *against* each step — because the arguments against are what
interviewers actually ask about.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This ladder is for pipelines you build yourself.** If the text is going into
a pre-trained model, stay with the tokenizer and the preprocessing assumptions
that model was trained under; adding the steps below on your own moves your
input away from the form the model expects.
:::

| Step | [What it buys you]{.pro} | [What it costs you]{.con} | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercasing | `Pump` = `pump`: two columns merge into one and their counts add up | `US` → `us`, `Apple` → `apple`. Loses proper nouns and acronyms — and in Turkish `str.lower()` is outright wrong, silently. | Yes for English; elsewhere only with a locale-aware function |
| Punctuation stripping | `fail;` = `fail` | Destroys `P-101`, decimals, URLs, chemical formulas. | No — strip selectively |
| Stop word removal | drops `the`, `is`, `of`; 43.9% of tokens here | Destroys negation (`not`), and phrases like *to be or not to be*. | Only for sparse count models |
| Stemming | `replaced` → `replac`, collapsing inflections cheaply | Crude suffix chopping. `university` → `univers` = `universe`. | No |
| Lemmatization | `replaced` → `replace`, correctly | Needs a dictionary and part-of-speech tagging, and is slow. | Usually not for transformer input; consider it for sparse and linguistic tasks |

: The normalization ladder {tbl-colwidths="[14,28,40,18]"}

That first row hides a trap worth naming here, because it costs nothing to
avoid and everything to miss. Python's `str.lower()` implements the Unicode
*default* case mapping — the language-independent one, which the standard
defines alongside language-specific tailorings that it does not apply unless
you ask. Turkish is one of the languages that needs a tailoring, because it has
two `i` letters and two `I` letters:

```python
"İSTANBUL".lower()              # 'i̇stanbul' — 'i' + U+0307, nine characters
"İSTANBUL".lower() == "istanbul"  # False
"IĞDIR".lower()                 # 'iğdir' — should be 'ığdır'
```

Nothing errors. The result simply lands in a different vocabulary column from
the word a user types, forever. @sec-bake-off hits this bug on a real corpus and
@sec-turkish-nlp gives the locale-aware fix; the point *here* is only that
"lowercasing" is a language-dependent operation being presented as a free one.

Read the last column with suspicion: it is a default, not a rule. Every one
of these steps is a bet that the distinction it erases does not matter for
*your* task. Lowercasing is usually free in topic classification and removes
a useful cue in named entity recognition, where capitalisation is part of the
signal. The only way to settle it is to try both and measure.

Stemming and lemmatization both aim at the same thing — collapsing
inflected forms — but they are not the same operation. Stemming
[@porter1980algorithm] applies rewrite rules and does not care whether the
result is a word. Lemmatization returns the dictionary form and needs to
know that `left` is the past tense of `leave` in one sentence and a
direction in another.

The honest modern answer to "which should I use?" depends on the pipeline. If
you are feeding a pretrained transformer, use the model's own tokenizer and do
neither: subword tokenization (below) already handles the rare-word half of what
stemming was for. Be precise about what that does *not* do, though — subwords
split a rare word into pieces; they do not collapse `kullanıyorum` and
`kullandık` into one shared column. Where you need that — lexical search, a
sparse classifier, anything counting term matches — a stemmer is still doing
real work, and @sec-turkish-nlp measures it taking Turkish recall@1 from 28.0%
to 95.3%. Either way you should be able to explain the distinction, because it
is one of the most reliably asked questions in the field.

::: {#gloss-stop-word .column-margin .term-gloss}
**stop word** — a word so common that some pipelines throw it away
before counting anything. *The*, *of*, *is*. Whether that is a saving or
a mistake depends entirely on the task. [↩](#term-stop-word){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-vocabulary .column-margin .term-gloss}
**vocabulary** — the finite set of token ids a tokenizer can emit. A word
does not have to be in it whole: the tokenizer can split it into smaller
pieces that are. [↩](#term-vocabulary){.term-back}
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**[Stop word](#gloss-stop-word){#term-stop-word .term-ref} removal is not free.** On the corpus used later in this chapter,
`scikit-learn`'s English stop word list contains 318 entries. Those 318
words are **0.4% of the [vocabulary](#gloss-vocabulary){#term-vocabulary .term-ref}** but **43.9% of all tokens**. You are
deleting nearly half your text. That is a real compression win for a sparse
model — and a catastrophe if the signal you need is in the word *not*.
:::

### Subwords: the compromise that won {#sec-text-as-data-bpe}

::: {#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .column-margin .term-gloss}
**byte-pair encoding (BPE)** — a way of learning the token list from the
text itself: start from single characters (or bytes), and keep gluing together
whichever pair occurs most often. [↩](#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){.term-back}
:::

Word-level tokenization has a problem it cannot solve on its own: the vocabulary never
closes. Character-level tokenization has the opposite problem: sequences
become very long and each unit means almost nothing. [Byte-pair encoding]{.hl}
([BPE](#gloss-byte-pair-encoding-bpe){#term-byte-pair-encoding-bpe .term-ref}) splits the difference by *learning* its units from data
[@sennrich2016neural].

The algorithm is surprisingly simple. Start with characters. Count every
adjacent pair. Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol. Repeat. Those
four steps are the whole of BPE.

```python
from collections import Counter

corpus = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
words = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): n for w, n in corpus.items()}

def pair_counts(words):
    pairs = Counter()
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pairs[(a, b)] += freq
    return pairs

def merge(words, pair):
    a, b = pair
    out = {}
    for symbols, freq in words.items():
        new, i = [], 0
        while i < len(symbols):
            if i < len(symbols) - 1 and symbols[i] == a and symbols[i + 1] == b:
                new.append(a + b)
                i += 2
            else:
                new.append(symbols[i])
                i += 1
        out[tuple(new)] = freq
    return out

merges = []
for step in range(1, 11):
    best, count = pair_counts(words).most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(best)
    words = merge(words, best)
    print(f"merge {step:>2}: {best[0]!r} + {best[1]!r} -> "
          f"{best[0] + best[1]!r}  (seen {count} times)")
```

```text
merge  1: 'e' + 's' -> 'es'  (seen 9 times)
merge  2: 'es' + 't' -> 'est'  (seen 9 times)
merge  3: 'est' + '</w>' -> 'est</w>'  (seen 9 times)
merge  4: 'l' + 'o' -> 'lo'  (seen 7 times)
merge  5: 'lo' + 'w' -> 'low'  (seen 7 times)
merge  6: 'n' + 'e' -> 'ne'  (seen 6 times)
merge  7: 'ne' + 'w' -> 'new'  (seen 6 times)
merge  8: 'new' + 'est</w>' -> 'newest</w>'  (seen 6 times)
merge  9: 'low' + '</w>' -> 'low</w>'  (seen 5 times)
merge 10: 'w' + 'i' -> 'wi'  (seen 3 times)
```

Look at what happened without anyone supplying a grammar. The algorithm's
first two merges build `est` — the English superlative suffix — and the third
attaches the word boundary to it, because superlatives are frequent. It discovered `low` and `new` as stems.
[Nobody told it that English has suffixes.]{.hl} It counted. A boundary
landing on a real suffix helps here, but it is not guaranteed: BPE optimises
frequency patterns, not morphology.

The payoff is what happens to a word the model has never seen. To tokenize,
we replay the learned merges in the order they were learned:

```python
def apply_merges(word, merges):
    symbols = tuple(word) + ("</w>",)
    for pair in merges:
        symbols = tuple(merge({symbols: 1}, pair).keys())[0]
    return symbols

for w in ["lowest", "newer", "slow", "widest"]:
    print(f"{w:<8} -> {' '.join(apply_merges(w, merges))}")
```

```text
lowest   -> low est</w>
newer    -> new e r </w>
slow     -> s low</w>
widest   -> wi d est</w>
```

`lowest` never appeared in training, and it is segmented into two units the
model knows well. This is the main reason subwords won: **if the starting
alphabet covers every character of a word — or the tokenizer falls back to
bytes — an unseen *word* does not have to become one `<UNK>`**. In the worst
case it falls back to shorter pieces, as `slow` partly does. Representation
quality drops; the input does not become unrepresentable.

That condition — every *character* of the new word being in the alphabet the
merges were learned over — is where real tokenizers differ from this toy, and
@sec-text-as-data-bytes takes it up after the figure.

```{ojs}
viewof bpeWord = Inputs.text({
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Verbatim output of the merge loop at the top of this section — if the toy
// corpus changes, regenerate both together.
bpeMerges = [
  ["e", "s"], ["es", "t"], ["est", "</w>"], ["l", "o"], ["lo", "w"],
  ["n", "e"], ["ne", "w"], ["new", "est</w>"], ["low", "</w>"], ["w", "i"]
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bpeTrace = {
  const raw = (bpeWord || "").toLowerCase();
  const clean = raw.replace(/[^a-z]/g, "");
  const dropped = raw.length !== clean.length;
  let symbols = clean.length ? [...clean, "</w>"] : [];
  const trace = [{ step: 0, rule: "start (characters)", symbols: [...symbols] }];
  bpeMerges.forEach(([a, b], k) => {
    const out = [];
    let i = 0, used = false;
    while (i < symbols.length) {
      if (i < symbols.length - 1 && symbols[i] === a && symbols[i + 1] === b) {
        out.push(a + b); i += 2; used = true;
      } else { out.push(symbols[i]); i += 1; }
    }
    symbols = out;
    if (used) trace.push({ step: k + 1, rule: `${a} + ${b}`, symbols: [...symbols] });
  });
  trace.dropped = dropped;
  return trace;
}
```

### Characters or bytes: what BPE starts from {#sec-text-as-data-bytes}

This section in one sentence: a character-based starting alphabet has an
open-ended Unicode coverage problem, while a byte-based one can represent any
text with 256 values.

The loop above — count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent, repeat — *is*
BPE. The name is older than its use in NLP: it comes from a 1994 data-compression
algorithm that kept replacing the most frequent pair of adjacent **bytes** in a
file with a single byte value the file did not use [@gage1994new]. Sennrich and
colleagues kept the loop and changed its purpose: the merges build a vocabulary
instead of shrinking a file, and the merge list is kept so it can be replayed
on new text [@sennrich2016neural].

That leaves one decision the loop does not make for you: **what the starting
symbols are**. It is a separate choice from the algorithm. BPE, WordPiece and
Unigram (@sec-text-as-data-algorithms) decide *how* units are learned;
characters or bytes decide *what they are built from*.

**Starting from characters.** This is what the toy above did, and it has a
hole. The merge table can only combine symbols it has seen, and the alphabet
this one saw came from four English words. So an unseen **character** still
breaks it: `apply_merges("çay", merges)` returns `('ç', 'a', 'y', '</w>')`, and
`ç`, `a` and `y` are not in the vocabulary. A real character-level tokenizer
needs every character it may ever meet in its starting alphabet, and Unicode
defines well over a hundred thousand of them. The rare ones become `<UNK>`.

**Starting from bytes.** Computers do not store characters; they store bytes.
Two layers are involved. Unicode gives every character a number, its **code
point**, written `U+` followed by the number in hexadecimal: `ç` is U+00E7.
An *encoding* then decides which bytes store that number. UTF-8, the standard
encoding for text on the web, writes each code point as one to four bytes.
ASCII letters take one byte; the Turkish letters `ç`, `ş`, `ğ`, `ı`, `ö`, `ü`
and `İ` take two; most Chinese characters take three and most emoji four:

```python
for ch in ["a", "ç", "ş", "İ", "世", "😀"]:
    b = ch.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{ch}  U+{ord(ch):04X}  {len(b)} byte(s): {' '.join(f'{x:02X}' for x in b)}")
```

```text
a  U+0061  1 byte(s): 61
ç  U+00E7  2 byte(s): C3 A7
ş  U+015F  2 byte(s): C5 9F
İ  U+0130  2 byte(s): C4 B0
世  U+4E16  3 byte(s): E4 B8 96
😀  U+1F600  4 byte(s): F0 9F 98 80
```

A byte has only 256 possible values, so an alphabet of 256 bytes is closed:
every string in every language is a sequence of them. Byte-level BPE runs
exactly the same merge loop over byte sequences instead of characters
[@radford2019language]. Frequent byte pairs merge back into whole characters
first — the two bytes of `ç` become one token early if the training text holds
enough Turkish — and then into subwords, as before.

Here is a byte-level tokenizer, OpenAI's `cl100k_base`, showing the bytes behind
each token. `enc.encode` returns a list of integer token ids — those integers,
not strings, are what the model receives — and `decode_single_token_bytes`
shows the bytes each id stands for:

```python
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
for text in ["çay", "şişe", "ŞİŞE", "😀"]:
    pieces = [enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t) for t in enc.encode(text)]
    print(f"{text:<5} {len(pieces)} tokens  {pieces}")
```

```text
çay   2 tokens  [b'\xc3\xa7', b'ay']
şişe  3 tokens  [b'\xc5\x9fi', b'\xc5\x9f', b'e']
ŞİŞE  6 tokens  [b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'\xc4\xb0', b'\xc5', b'\x9e', b'E']
😀     2 tokens  [b'\xf0\x9f\x98', b'\x80']
```

Read three things in that output. `ç` is a single token, because its two bytes
were frequent enough to merge. `ŞİŞE` costs twice as many tokens as `şişe`:
capital `Ş` was rare in training, its two bytes never merged, and each of those
tokens holds *half a character* — `b'\xc5'` is not valid text on its own. The
emoji is split the same way. Nothing ever becomes `<UNK>`; rare characters just
become expensive.

| | Character-level BPE | Byte-level BPE |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Starting alphabet | every character in the training text — thousands for multilingual data | the 256 byte values, always |
| A character never seen in training | [`<UNK>`, unless a byte fallback is added]{.con} | [cannot happen: it is spelled out in bytes]{.pro} |
| What one token holds | [whole characters]{.pro} | [bytes — sometimes only part of a character]{.con} |
| Cost of a rare character | [one symbol]{.pro} | [up to four tokens, one per byte]{.con} |
| Scripts covered | whatever the training text contained | every script, by construction |

: Characters or bytes as the starting alphabet {tbl-colwidths="[26,37,37]"}

There is a middle road, **byte fallback**: keep a character-level vocabulary and
spell out in bytes only the characters it lacks. The SentencePiece library
offers it as an option.

**Which one is used today.** For the large generative models most people call
through an API, byte-level BPE is the default. GPT-2 introduced it with a
50,257-token vocabulary [@radford2019language]. OpenAI's `cl100k_base` and
`o200k_base`, measured in the next section, are byte-level. Llama 3 moved to a
128K-token vocabulary that combines 100K tokens from OpenAI's `tiktoken` with 28K
added for non-English languages [@grattafiori2024llama3]. BERT and its close
relatives such as DistilBERT and ELECTRA still ship WordPiece over characters
[@devlin2019bert] (RoBERTa, although built on BERT, switched to GPT-2's
byte-level BPE), and the
table in @sec-text-as-data-algorithms shows which algorithm ships where. The
practical rule does not depend on any of this: use the tokenizer the model was
trained with, and count tokens with it.

Two questions are worth keeping apart here. A byte-level design guarantees
**coverage**: any Unicode character can be represented, so a Turkish word does
not become `<UNK>`. How *many* tokens a language costs is a separate question,
and UTF-8 byte counts do not settle it on their own: it depends on how often
that language's characters and sequences appear in the tokenizer's training
data, on the merge statistics, and on how much of the vocabulary budget goes to
that language. The next section measures that difference for Turkish.

### Who pays for Turkish {#sec-text-as-data-turkish}

Now the part that matters if you work in a language other than English. A
tokenizer is trained on a corpus, and how efficiently it encodes a language
depends on how much of that language the corpus contained — which, for the
tokenizers most people use, means mostly English. The consequence is
measurable. Here is Article 1 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, in the official English and Turkish texts, run
through OpenAI's tokenizers:

```python
import tiktoken

en = ("All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. "
      "They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards "
      "one another in a spirit of brotherhood.")
tr = ("Bütün insanlar hür, haysiyet ve haklar bakımından eşit doğarlar. "
      "Akıl ve vicdana sahiptirler ve birbirlerine karşı kardeşlik "
      "zihniyeti ile hareket etmelidirler.")

for name in ["cl100k_base", "o200k_base"]:
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    a, b = len(enc.encode(en)), len(enc.encode(tr))
    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  english : {len(en):>4} chars -> {a:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(en) / a:4.2f} chars/token)")
    print(f"  turkish : {len(tr):>4} chars -> {b:>3} tokens  "
          f"({len(tr) / b:4.2f} chars/token)")
    print(f"  turkish costs {b / a:4.2f}x more tokens")
```

```text
cl100k_base:
  english :  170 chars ->  33 tokens  (5.15 chars/token)
  turkish :  160 chars ->  60 tokens  (2.67 chars/token)
  turkish costs 1.82x more tokens
o200k_base:
  english :  170 chars ->  33 tokens  (5.15 chars/token)
  turkish :  160 chars ->  46 tokens  (3.48 chars/token)
  turkish costs 1.39x more tokens
```

The same sentence, the same meaning, [1.82× the tokens]{.hl} on the
GPT-3.5/4 tokenizer. Since APIs bill per token and context windows are
measured in tokens, a Turkish speaker pays more money for less context.
Newer tokenizers narrow the gap (1.39× with `o200k_base`) but do not close
it. This is a documented and measured unfairness across languages
[@petrov2023language], not a rounding error. One sentence does not give you a
universal coefficient: these numbers show only how differently the same
content can be split in two languages. Nor is the source of the gap merely
that Turkish characters take two bytes — the language mix in the tokenizer's
training data and the vocabulary budget matter just as much.

Why does it happen? Turkish encodes far more grammatical information inside a
single word, with suffixes, than English does [@oflazer1994two], so one stem
produces many surface forms. English spreads the same information across
separate words more often, and that is exactly what a frequency-based merge
algorithm captures well. Here is one Turkish stem growing suffix by suffix,
again on `cl100k_base`; each word is encoded with a leading space, the way it
would appear inside a sentence:

```text
ev             1 tokens  [' ev']
evler          2 tokens  [' ev', 'ler']
evlerimiz      4 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz']
evlerimizden   5 tokens  [' ev', 'ler', 'im', 'iz', 'den']
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The accent-coloured box is the stem; the rest are suffixes byte-pair encoding
learned to split off because they recur, not because anyone described Turkish
to it. Reading left to right, the token count is also the invoice: the
longest form costs five tokens where its three-word English translation costs
three.
:::
::::

Read that output again, because it is remarkable in two opposite ways.

The bad news first. One Turkish word costs five tokens, where its English
translation *from our houses* costs three — English needed three separate
words to say it and still paid fewer tokens.

Now the good news, with one honest asterisk. Look at *where* it split.
`ev|ler|im|iz|den` lines up with the real morphology at three of its four
boundaries — *ev* (house), *-ler* (plural), *-den* (from) — and nobody supplied
a rule of Turkish grammar. The asterisk is `im|iz`: *-imiz* ("our") is a
**single** morpheme that BPE has cut in half, because `im` and `iz` are each
frequent on their own. That is why the figure above puts a dash under `iz`
rather than a gloss. The newer `o200k_base` happens to keep `imiz` whole
(`ev|ler|imiz|den`, four tokens), which shows that the exact cut depends on the
merge table, not on the language. Frequency is a good proxy for morphology, not
a substitute for it — and at equal vocabulary size, unigram LM segments closer to morphology
than BPE does [@bostrom2020byte].

Two conventions collide in those outputs, and they are worth naming. GPT's BPE
tokenizers and BERT's WordPiece do not run on the raw string. They first
**pre-tokenize** it: they split it on whitespace and punctuation (GPT-2 does
this with a regular expression), and only then split each piece into subwords.
SentencePiece deliberately does not pre-tokenize. It is built to run on the raw
string, which is what makes it work on languages that do not put spaces between
words. Where a pre-tokenizer is used, word boundaries have to survive into the
token itself, or detokenization (turning tokens back into text) would be
ambiguous. GPT's encodings attach the
preceding space to the token — hence `' ev'` above, with a leading space —
while SentencePiece [@kudo2018sentencepiece] substitutes a visible marker,
`▁ev`. Same idea, two spellings; the figure uses the `▁` form because it is
easier to see on a page.

One more, to show that diacritics cost extra (still `cl100k_base`, this time
without a leading space):

```text
gorusebileceklerimiz            8 tokens  ['gor','use','b','ile','cek','ler','im','iz']
görüşebileceklerimiz           10 tokens  ['g','ör','ü','ş','eb','ile','cek','ler','im','iz']
```

On this word, writing correct Turkish costs 25% more than writing ASCII
Turkish — ten tokens against eight. The direction is general; the exact factor
is not, and it depends on the tokenizer and on which letters the text uses.

Before you trust that number, one step has to happen that nobody mentions. `ö`
can be stored two ways: as a single code point (U+00F6, "NFC") or as `o`
followed by a combining diaeresis (U+0308, "NFD"). The two are indistinguishable
on screen, compare as *unequal* in Python, and cost different numbers of tokens
— `görüşebileceklerimiz` is 20 characters and 23 bytes in NFC, 23 characters and
26 bytes in NFD, and on `cl100k_base` it costs 10 tokens in NFC but 15 in NFD.
macOS filenames, many PDF extractions and some web forms hand
you NFD. So the first line of any pipeline that touches non-ASCII text is:

```python
import unicodedata
text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)
```

Every measurement in this section was taken after that call. Skip it and your
vocabulary quietly contains two spellings of the same word. You will also meet
**NFKC**, a stronger form that additionally folds "compatibility" variants —
the ligature `ﬁ` into `fi`, full-width `Ａ` into `A` — and which SentencePiece
applies by default, in a slightly extended form. It changes more than NFC does,
so use it deliberately.

The ASCII comparison above is not an optimisation suggestion. Stripping Turkish
characters damages search quality, user experience and meaning distinctions;
what we measured is the tokenizer's behaviour. Write correct Turkish anyway;
just know what it costs, and never benchmark a multilingual system on token
counts alone.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why not just use characters and skip all this?

A character vocabulary is tiny (~100 symbols for English, 256 if you work in
bytes), has no out-of-vocabulary problem once the character set is closed —
which bytes guarantee and a hand-picked alphabet does not — and needs no
training. So why does everyone use subwords?

Cut the Turkish text of Article 1 from above three ways, and count:

```python
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
units = {
    "characters": list(tr),
    "subword tokens": [enc.decode([t]) for t in enc.encode(tr)],
    "words": tr.split(),
}
for name, seq in units.items():
    n = len(seq)
    print(f"{name:<15} {n:>3} units  {n * n:>6,} pairs  first six: {seq[:6]}")
```

```text
characters      160 units  25,600 pairs  first six: ['B', 'ü', 't', 'ü', 'n', ' ']
subword tokens   60 units   3,600 pairs  first six: ['B', 'üt', 'ün', ' insan', 'lar', ' h']
words            21 units     441 pairs  first six: ['Bütün', 'insanlar', 'hür,', 'haysiyet', 've', 'haklar']
```

**The first reason is sequence length.** Attention compares every position
with every other position (@sec-transformers), so a sequence of $n$ units costs
$n^2$ comparisons — the `pairs` column. 160 characters make 25,600 pairs; the
same text as 60 subword tokens makes 3,600. The sequence got 2.7× shorter and
the comparisons 7.1× fewer. The rest of a transformer layer grows only
linearly, so lengthening a sequence 5× costs somewhere between 5× and 25×
depending on where you sit relative to the model width — and the quadratic
term is the one that eventually wins.

**The second is what one unit carries.** Read the first six units of each row.
`ü` and `t` say nothing about the sentence; a model fed characters has to spend
its first layers rebuilding pieces like `insan` ("human") before it can use
them. The subword row hands it ` insan` and `lar` directly.

**Words are shorter still, but they fail another way.** 21 units and 441 pairs
look ideal, until you notice that `hür,` with its comma is a different entry
from `hür`, and that every new combination of suffixes is a new word. The next
example shows what that does to a word the vocabulary has not seen.

Subwords are a compression scheme: they buy shorter sequences by spending
vocabulary. The tokenizer is the knob that trades vocabulary size against
sequence length, and BPE sets that knob using the statistics of the data rather
than a human's guess.
:::

### Characters, subwords, whole words: one example {#sec-text-as-data-granularities}

The table below compares the three choices on paper. First, watch all three on
one small example, so that every row of the table is something you have seen
happen.

The corpus is sixty Turkish words: twelve stems, each on its own and with the
same four endings (`-ler`, `-de`, `-den`, `-lerde`), spelled with vowel harmony
(`-ler`/`-lar`, `-de`/`-da`). The two test
words, `evlerden` ("from the houses") and `okullardan` ("from the schools"),
appear nowhere in it, although every piece of them does. Each tokenizer learns
from the corpus and then splits the two new words. The BPE line reuses
`pair_counts`, `merge` and `apply_merges` from @sec-text-as-data-bpe:

```python
stems = {"ev": "e", "el": "e", "göl": "e", "köy": "e", "gün": "e", "yüz": "e",
         "okul": "a", "yol": "a", "kol": "a", "yıl": "a", "kız": "a", "masa": "a"}
corpus = {}
for stem, v in stems.items():          # v: the vowel the suffixes take
    for suffix, n in [("", 4), (f"l{v}r", 2), (f"d{v}", 4),
                      (f"d{v}n", 4), (f"l{v}rd{v}", 4)]:
        corpus[stem + suffix] = n      # ev, evler, evde, evden, evlerde, ...
test = ["evlerden", "okullardan"]      # neither word is in the corpus

chars = sorted({c for word in corpus for c in word})
words = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): n for w, n in corpus.items()}
merges = []
while len(chars) + 1 + len(merges) < 60:   # stop at a 60-symbol vocabulary
    best, _ = pair_counts(words).most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(best)
    words = merge(words, best)

tokenizers = {
    "whole words": (len(corpus), lambda w: [w if w in corpus else "<UNK>"]),
    "characters": (len(chars), lambda w: list(w)),
    "subwords (BPE)": (len(chars) + 1 + len(merges),
                       lambda w: list(apply_merges(w, merges))),
}
for name, (size, split) in tokenizers.items():
    pieces = [p for w in test for p in split(w)]
    print(f"{name:<15} vocabulary {size:>2}   {len(pieces):>2} units: {' '.join(pieces)}")
```

```text
whole words     vocabulary 60    2 units: <UNK> <UNK>
characters      vocabulary 18   18 units: e v l e r d e n o k u l l a r d a n
subwords (BPE)  vocabulary 60    6 units: ev ler den</w> okul lar dan</w>
```

Now read that output against the rows of the table below:

- **Vocabulary size.** Whole words already need 60 entries for twelve stems and
  four suffixes, and real Turkish stems take far more than four suffix
  combinations. Characters need 18. BPE was capped at 60: the 18 letters, the
  end-of-word marker `</w>`, and 41 learned merges.
- **Out-of-vocabulary words.** The whole-word tokenizer turns both test words
  into `<UNK>`, so the model receives nothing. The other two never produce
  `<UNK>`, because every letter of the new words is in their alphabet.
- **Sequence length.** The same two words are 18 units as characters, 6 as
  subwords and 2 as whole words.
- **Meaning per unit.** `e`, `v` and `l` mean nothing on their own. `ev`
  ("house"), `ler` (plural) and `den` ("from") are exactly the meaningful parts
  of the word; `</w>` only marks where the word ends.
- **Morphologically rich languages.** BPE found the stem and both suffixes of
  words it had never seen, by counting alone.
- **Needs training.** Only the BPE line ran a learning loop. The other two just
  listed what they saw.

The three choices, side by side. Before the table, the summary worth
remembering:

- **Word level:** short sequences, a large and open-ended vocabulary.
- **Character/byte level:** a small closed vocabulary, long sequences.
- **Subword:** a compromise between the two, learned from data.

Every tokenizer you will ever meet sits somewhere on this line, and the whole
design problem is that the two ends fail in opposite directions.

| | Characters | Subwords (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) | Whole words |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vocabulary size | [~100 for ASCII; tens of thousands for multilingual Unicode — 256 if you work in bytes]{.pro} | roughly 30k–250k | [Unbounded — it never closes]{.con} |
| Out-of-vocabulary words | [Cannot arise *if* the character set is closed — guaranteed only when you work in bytes]{.pro} | [Rare — an unrecognised word falls back to shorter pieces, provided the vocabulary covers every character or falls back to bytes. WordPiece without that fallback still emits `[UNK]`]{.pro} | [Constant, and worst for the words you care about]{.con} |
| Sequence length | [~2.5–5× longer than subwords, ~6–8× longer than words (the Article 1 measurement); long sequences are both slower and more expensive]{.con} | [Moderate]{.pro} | [Shortest]{.pro} |
| Meaning per unit | [Almost none — `p` means nothing]{.con} | Partial; often morpheme-like | [A whole unit of meaning]{.pro} |
| Morphologically rich languages | Handles them, expensively | [Handles them well — it recovered Turkish suffixes above]{.pro} | [Falls seriously short here]{.con} |
| Needs training | [No]{.pro} | [Yes, on a corpus]{.con} | [No]{.pro} |

: Three tokenization granularities {tbl-colwidths="[24,20,30,26]"}

Subwords are not best on any single row, but unlike the other two they have no
weakness bad enough to rule them out on its own. That is why most modern
language models prefer them: they largely remove the word level's
out-of-vocabulary problem while keeping sequences far shorter than characters
would.

### Three ways to learn the same kind of unit {#sec-text-as-data-algorithms}

BPE is one of three algorithms you will meet. Their core ideas fit on one line
each:

| Method | Core idea |
|---|---|
| BPE | merge the most frequent adjacent pair |
| WordPiece | score how much a merge helps, relative to its parts |
| Unigram LM | start from a large set of pieces and prune it probabilistically |

: The three algorithms in one sentence each {tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

**All three produce subwords; what differs is which pieces they count as
"good" enough to keep.** `SentencePiece` [@kudo2018sentencepiece] is not a
fourth algorithm but a *toolkit* that can run BPE or Unigram LM — Llama 2 and
Gemma use it in BPE mode, T5 and ALBERT in Unigram mode. That distinction is
worth making before the comparison starts. The table below spells out what each
one optimises, and knowing which one a model uses is how you predict its
splits. One caveat about the WordPiece row: the original training procedure is
not published in full, and this ratio is the common approximate reconstruction
used to explain its logic.

| | What it optimises | Direction | Ships in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BPE** [@sennrich2016neural] | merge the most *frequent* adjacent pair | bottom-up, the vocabulary grows | GPT-2/3/4, RoBERTa, Llama, Gemma |
| **WordPiece** [@schuster2012japanese] | merge the pair that most increases corpus likelihood, roughly maximising $\frac{c(ab)}{c(a)\,c(b)}$ | bottom-up | BERT, DistilBERT, ELECTRA |
| **Unigram LM** [@kudo2018subword] | start from a large candidate set and *prune* the pieces whose removal costs least likelihood, re-estimating piece probabilities by EM (expectation–maximization) | top-down, the vocabulary shrinks | T5, ALBERT, XLNet, XLM-R |

: Three subword algorithms, and what each one is actually maximising
{tbl-colwidths="[16,40,24,20]"}

#### One corpus, three algorithms

The table says what each algorithm maximises. Here is what that means on the
sixty-word corpus from @sec-text-as-data-granularities, with the same two
unseen words and the same budget of 60 vocabulary entries. The code is a
minimal version of each: WordPiece with the scoring rule in the table, and a
simplified Unigram LM that re-estimates its piece probabilities from the single
best split of each word instead of running full EM.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: minimal WordPiece and Unigram LM

```python
import math

def train_wordpiece(corpus, size):
    words = {tuple([w[0]] + ["##" + c for c in w[1:]]): n for w, n in corpus.items()}
    vocab = {s for symbols in words for s in symbols}
    first = None
    while len(vocab) < size:
        pairs, single = Counter(), Counter()
        for symbols, n in words.items():
            for s in symbols:
                single[s] += n
            for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
                pairs[(a, b)] += n
        score = {p: c / (single[p[0]] * single[p[1]]) for p, c in pairs.items()}
        best = max(score, key=lambda p: (score[p], p))
        first = first or (pairs, score)
        glued = best[0] + best[1].removeprefix("##")
        new = {}
        for symbols, n in words.items():
            out, i = [], 0
            while i < len(symbols):
                if symbols[i:i + 2] == best:
                    out.append(glued)
                    i += 2
                else:
                    out.append(symbols[i])
                    i += 1
            new[tuple(out)] = n
        words, vocab = new, vocab | {glued}
    return vocab, first

def wordpiece_split(word, vocab):          # greedy: longest known piece first
    pieces, start = [], 0
    while start < len(word):
        for end in range(len(word), start, -1):
            piece = word[start:end] if start == 0 else "##" + word[start:end]
            if piece in vocab:
                break
        else:
            return ["[UNK]"]
        pieces.append(piece)
        start = end
    return pieces

def best_split(word, logp):                # Viterbi: the most probable split
    best = [(0.0, [])] + [(-math.inf, None)] * len(word)
    for end in range(1, len(word) + 1):
        for start in range(end):
            piece = word[start:end]
            if piece in logp and best[start][1] is not None:
                score = best[start][0] + logp[piece]
                if score > best[end][0]:
                    best[end] = (score, best[start][1] + [piece])
    return best[-1]

def train_unigram(corpus, size):
    counts = Counter()                     # start big: every substring
    for w, n in corpus.items():
        for i in range(len(w)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(w) + 1):
                counts[w[i:j]] += n
    start_size = len(counts)
    logprobs = lambda c: {p: math.log(k / sum(c.values())) for p, k in c.items()}
    loss = lambda lp: -sum(n * best_split(w, lp)[0] for w, n in corpus.items())
    while len(counts) > size:
        lp = logprobs(counts)
        base = loss(lp)
        cost = {p: loss({q: v for q, v in lp.items() if q != p}) - base
                for p in counts if len(p) > 1}     # single letters always stay
        k = max(1, min(len(counts) - size, len(cost) // 5))
        for p in sorted(cost, key=lambda p: (cost[p], p))[:k]:
            del counts[p]                  # prune the pieces that cost least
        lp = logprobs(counts)              # re-estimate from the best splits
        counts = Counter({p: 0.001 for p in counts})
        for w, n in corpus.items():
            for piece in best_split(w, lp)[1]:
                counts[piece] += n
    return logprobs(counts), start_size
```
:::

```python
wp_vocab, (pairs, score) = train_wordpiece(corpus, 60)
uni_logp, start_size = train_unigram(corpus, 60)

print("first step, the same starting pairs:")
print("  highest count (BPE):      ",
      [(a + b.removeprefix("##"), c) for (a, b), c in pairs.most_common(3)])
print("  highest score (WordPiece):",
      [(a + b.removeprefix("##"), round(s, 3))
       for (a, b), s in sorted(score.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:3]])
print(f"  Unigram LM starts from {start_size} substrings and prunes to {len(uni_logp)}")
print()
for w in test:
    print(f"{w:<11} BPE       : {' | '.join(apply_merges(w, merges))}")
    print(f"{'':<11} WordPiece : {' | '.join(wordpiece_split(w, wp_vocab))}")
    print(f"{'':<11} Unigram LM: {' | '.join(best_split(w, uni_logp)[1])}")
```

```text
first step, the same starting pairs:
  highest count (BPE):       [('##de', 72), ('##da', 72), ('##rd', 48)]
  highest score (WordPiece): [('ok', 0.056), ('##ku', 0.056), ('ev', 0.028)]
  Unigram LM starts from 322 substrings and prunes to 60

evlerden    BPE       : ev | ler | den</w>
            WordPiece : ev | ##l | ##e | ##r | ##d | ##e | ##n
            Unigram LM: evlerde | n
okullardan  BPE       : okul | lar | dan</w>
            WordPiece : okullar | ##d | ##a | ##n
            Unigram LM: okullarda | n
```

**BPE** merges the most *frequent* pair. `d` + `e` occurs 72 times in the
corpus, so BPE's vocabulary fills with pieces that many words share — `de`,
`ler`, `den`, `lar`, `dan` — and the unseen words split exactly at their
suffixes.

**WordPiece** starts from the same pairs but divides each count by how often
its two parts occur at all, $\frac{c(ab)}{c(a)\,c(b)}$. `o` + `k` wins with
0.056 instead of `d` + `e`, not because it is frequent but because the two
symbols never occur apart: a word-initial `o` followed by `##k` appears only in
`okul`. The rule rewards letters that stick together, so WordPiece spends its
budget growing stems from the left — `ok`, `oku`, `okul`, `okull`, `okullar` —
and never builds a suffix piece such as `##den`. The `##` marks a piece that
continues a word. To split a new word, WordPiece does not replay merges: it
takes the longest piece it knows from the left, then the longest piece after
that. For `okullardan` that is `okullar`, and after it only letters are left.

**Unigram LM** works in the other direction. It starts from every substring of
the corpus — 322 candidates — and keeps deleting the pieces it can lose most
cheaply, those whose removal lowers the probability of the corpus least, until
60 remain. On a corpus this small, keeping frequent whole forms such as
`evlerde` is the cheapest way to make the corpus probable, so `evlerden`
becomes `evlerde` + `n`. It is also the only one of the three that gives every
split a probability and picks the most probable one:

```python
def every_split(word, logp, prefix=()):
    if not word:
        yield sum(logp[p] for p in prefix), list(prefix)
    for end in range(1, len(word) + 1):
        if word[:end] in logp:
            yield from every_split(word[end:], logp, prefix + (word[:end],))

splits = sorted(every_split("evlerden", uni_logp), reverse=True)
print(f"{len(splits)} ways to split 'evlerden' with this vocabulary:")
for logp, pieces in splits:
    print(f"  p = {math.exp(logp):.1e}   {' | '.join(pieces)}")
```

```text
4 ways to split 'evlerden' with this vocabulary:
  p = 2.1e-03   evlerde | n
  p = 1.2e-14   evler | d | e | n
  p = 1.3e-22   ev | l | e | r | d | e | n
  p = 1.1e-31   e | v | l | e | r | d | e | n
```

The probability of a split is the product of its pieces' probabilities, so
every extra piece multiplies in another number below one. That is why the
two-piece split beats the eight-letter one by 28 orders of magnitude, and why
Unigram LM can also *sample* a less probable split during training — the
subword regularization described below.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: checking the minimal Unigram LM against SentencePiece

The minimal version above is not the library. Here is `sentencepiece` 0.2.2,
trained on the same corpus with the same 60-piece budget:

```python
import sentencepiece as spm

lines = [w for w, n in corpus.items() for _ in range(n)]
with open("corpus.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")

spm.SentencePieceTrainer.train(
    input="corpus.txt", model_prefix="uni", model_type="unigram", vocab_size=60,
    character_coverage=1.0, hard_vocab_limit=False, minloglevel=2,
    bos_id=-1, eos_id=-1, pad_id=-1)
uni = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file="uni.model")
for w in test:
    print(f"{w:<11} {' | '.join(uni.encode(w, out_type=str))}")
```

```text
evlerden    ▁evlerde | n
okullardan  ▁okul | l | a | r | d | a | n
```

`evlerden` gets the same split, `evlerde` + `n`; the library adds `▁` where a
word starts. `okullardan` does not: the library kept `okul` but not
`okullarda`, and spells the rest out letter by letter. The rule is the same; the
details of pruning and estimation are not.
:::

A sixty-word corpus exaggerates all of this. The rules are the real ones, but
with so little text a handful of counts decides every merge, and a 60-entry
vocabulary can hold whole words. Libraries also implement WordPiece training in
different ways; the ratio in the table is a common reconstruction of its rule.
For how the three compare on real corpora of millions of words, trust the
published measurement at the end of this section rather than this toy.

Two consequences worth carrying. First, WordPiece's ratio penalises pairs
whose parts are already common on their own — above, that is why it built stems
before suffixes. Second, Unigram LM is the only one that assigns a
*probability* to each segmentation rather than one deterministic answer, which
is what makes subword regularization possible: sample a different segmentation
each epoch and the model stops overfitting to one arbitrary split
[@kudo2018subword]. And the contribution of `SentencePiece`
[@kudo2018sentencepiece], the toolkit named above, shows up here: it treats the
raw string, spaces included, as the input, which is why its tokens carry a `▁`
where a space was.

The choice is not settled in BPE's favour, either: at equal vocabulary size,
unigram LM segments closer to morphology than BPE does, and models pretrained
with it matched or outperformed BPE-based ones on downstream tasks
[@bostrom2020byte].

## Zipf and Heaps: the long tail of words {#sec-text-as-data-zipf}

Everything above was mechanics — how to cut text, and what each cut costs.
This section is the two statistical facts underneath, the ones that explain why
the mechanics have to look like that at all. They are easy to conflate, so here
they are as two separate questions:

> **Question 1.** How are frequencies distributed between the commonest and the
> rarest words in a corpus? **Answer: Zipf's law.**
>
> **Question 2.** As you add more text, how does the number of distinct words
> grow? **Answer: Heaps' law.**

The answer to the second question is what makes tokenization hard — but the
first has to come first, because it is what explains the second.

### Zipf: how frequencies are distributed {#sec-text-as-data-zipf-distribution}

Take a real corpus — the 20 Newsgroups collection [@lang1995newsweeder],
11,314 documents, 2.29 million tokens — count every word, and sort by
frequency:

```python
from collections import Counter
import re
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups

docs = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="train",
                          remove=("headers", "footers", "quotes")).data
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", "\n".join(docs).lower())
counts = Counter(tokens)
print("tokens:", len(tokens), " distinct types:", len(counts))
```

```text
tokens: 2288401  distinct types: 78649
```

Now the shape of that distribution:

```text
top     10 types -> 20.99% of all tokens
top    100 types -> 46.99% of all tokens
top   1000 types -> 71.04% of all tokens
top  10000 types -> 92.50% of all tokens

types appearing exactly once: 38571  (49.0% of the vocabulary,
                                      1.69% of all tokens)
```

Ten words are a fifth of the corpus. Meanwhile [half the vocabulary appears
exactly once]{.hl}. Those single-occurrence words (*hapax legomena*) are
49% of everything you would have to store, and 1.7% of what you would ever
see. That one line is also why growing a word-level vocabulary to fix
out-of-vocabulary words does not scale: new data does not only raise the counts
of words you have, it keeps producing new types.

This is **Zipf's law** [@zipf1949human]: frequency falls off as a power of
rank, $f(r) \propto r^{-\alpha}$, which is close to a straight line on log-log
axes. "Close to" is doing work in that sentence. On this corpus the
tenth-ranked word appears 26,985 times, not the roughly 10,600 a clean
$\alpha = 1$ would predict (the top word's 106,425 divided by 10) — the head
of the distribution is flatter than the law, which is what Mandelbrot's
correction $f(r) \propto (r + b)^{-\alpha}$
exists to absorb. Take the straight line as a *shape*, not as a fitted model.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Deep dive: actually estimating the Zipf exponent

Reading a slope off a log-log rank-frequency plot with least squares is the
standard way to get a wrong power-law exponent, and it is wrong for three
separate reasons: ranking is a transform of the data, so rank and frequency are
mechanically correlated; the log transform makes the errors heteroscedastic,
which breaks the OLS assumption; and every point in the long, noisy tail counts
as much as the well-estimated head. The published fix is maximum likelihood
with a fitted lower cutoff $x_{\min}$, plus a Kolmogorov–Smirnov
goodness-of-fit test rather than an $R^2$ [@clauset2009powerlaw]. Nothing in
this chapter depends on the exact value; the shape is the lesson.
:::

Three consequences follow directly, and they shaped everything in modern NLP:

1. **A word-level vocabulary can never be complete.** New words arrive
   forever — names, part numbers, typos, compounds. This is the argument for
   subwords, in one sentence.
2. **Most of your vocabulary is statistically useless.** A word seen once
   supports no estimate of anything. This is why `min_df` exists, and why it
   cuts the matrix far more than stop word removal does.
3. **Frequency and informativeness are almost opposites.** The words you see
   most tell you least. That observation is the seed of the next section.

### Heaps: why the vocabulary keeps growing {#sec-text-as-data-heaps}

Zipf describes the corpus you already have. The second question above — *how many new words does the next million bring?* — needs a second law.
Count the distinct types as you walk through the corpus:

```python
import numpy as np

seen, curve = set(), []
for i, tok in enumerate(tokens, 1):
    seen.add(tok)
    if i % 10_000 == 0:
        curve.append((i, len(seen)))

N, V = np.array(curve).T
beta, logK = np.polyfit(np.log(N), np.log(V), 1)
print(f"|V| ~ {np.exp(logK):.1f} * N^{beta:.3f}")
```

This is **Heaps' law** [@heaps1978information]: vocabulary grows as a power of
corpus size, $|V| \approx K N^{\beta}$, with $\beta$ typically between 0.4 and
0.6. The exponent is below 1, so the curve keeps rising without ever reaching a
finite ceiling — the derivative $\mathrm{d}|V|/\mathrm{d}N = K\beta N^{\beta-1}$
is strictly positive for every $N$, while shrinking towards zero. It looks flat
on a plot while it is still growing, which is the trap.

[There is no corpus size at which you stop meeting new words. There is only a
size at which you stop meeting them *quickly*.]{.hl} That is the whole argument
for subwords, and it is also why `min_df` deletes most of your columns while
deleting very little of your text.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Always look at your top-50 list.** In this corpus the *second* most
frequent token is `'ax`, with 62,043 occurrences — ahead of *to*, *a*, and
*of*. It is not a word. It comes from 13 documents out of 11,314 — one quoted
copy of a corrupted binary posting and twelve replies that quoted it back, the
largest single document contributing 11,147 of the 62,043 occurrences.

Term frequency says `'ax` is the second most important word in the English
language. Document frequency says it appears in 0.1% of documents. That gap
between "appears often" and "appears in many places" is precisely what the
next section is built on — and it is a real bug that has been sitting in a
famous benchmark dataset for thirty years.

One nuance that sharpens the point rather than weakening it: the leading
apostrophe in `'ax` is *ours*. Our regex `[a-z']+` treats `'` as a word
character, so the corpus junk and our own tokenizer choice combine into this
particular string; under `scikit-learn`'s default `token_pattern` the same junk
surfaces as plain `ax`. The artefact is in the data, but its shape is a
preprocessing decision — which is the lesson of this whole section.
:::

One distinction to carry into the next section: a word can be very frequent
across the corpus yet concentrated in a handful of documents — `'ax` is exactly
that — while another word appears a little in almost every document. TF-IDF
uses precisely this difference: **frequency within a document** and
**spread across documents** are not the same thing.

## How a text becomes a vector {#sec-text-as-data-vectors}

This is the core of the chapter. We will take four short maintenance logs
all the way from strings to vectors you can compute distances on, skipping
no step and showing every intermediate number.

```python
corpus = [
    "the pump failed",           # d1
    "the pump was replaced",     # d2
    "the valve failed",          # d3
    "the seal leak was repaired", # d4
]
```

The whole chapter in one picture. Steps 1–3 turn text into a count vector and
throw away word order; steps 4–5 reweight and rescale it; step 6 compares. Every
number shown is the one the code actually produces for `d1 = "the pump failed"`.
The vocabulary index is alphabetical, so `failed` is column 0, `pump` is column 2
and `the` is column 6. The two accented boxes are the only places where any
*statistics* happen — everything else is bookkeeping.
:::
::::

### Step 1 — the vocabulary is just an index

There is no meaning in this step. We collect every distinct token, sort it,
and assign each one an integer. That integer is the word's *address*.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

cv = CountVectorizer()
X = cv.fit_transform(corpus)
print(cv.get_feature_names_out())
```

```text
['failed' 'leak' 'pump' 'repaired' 'replaced' 'seal' 'the' 'valve' 'was']
```

Nine words, so every vector from here on lives in $\mathbb{R}^9$. In real
word-level or n-gram systems the vocabulary typically runs from tens of
thousands into the hundreds of thousands, which is the whole difficulty.

### Step 2 — one-hot: a word as a vector, and why it is not enough

So we have an index. An index is not a vector, though, and we cannot do
arithmetic on a filing-cabinet drawer number. How do we turn a word into
something a model can actually compute with?

The simplest possible encoding of a single word: a vector of zeros with a
single 1 at the word's address.

```text
index of 'pump': 2
one-hot: [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
```

This is a legitimate vector, and it is almost useless on its own. Take the
dot product of *any* two distinct one-hot vectors and you get zero — the
single 1 in one vector always lands on a 0 in the other, so every product in
the sum is zero:

```text
pump  : [0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0]
valve : [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0]
        ------------------- multiply position by position
        [0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]  -> sum = 0
```

Under this encoding, `pump` is exactly as similar to `valve` as it is to
`repaired`. [Every word is orthogonal to every other word]{.hl} — the
representation contains no notion of similarity at all, only identity. It is
a filing system, not a meaning system: the vector for `pump` says *where the
word is kept*, and nothing about what it is like.

One-hot is used here as an intermediate structure — a way to see how a
document count vector is built, which is exactly the next step — not as the
final way to represent word meaning. Fixing that is the subject of
@sec-embeddings, where each word gets a dense vector that carries similarity
directly.

### Step 3 — a document is the sum of its one-hots

One word, one vector. But we did not set out to compare words — we set out to
compare *documents*, and a document is many words at once. What do we do with
all of them?

The simplest possible answer works: add them up. Add up the one-hot vectors of every token in a document and you get a count
vector. That is bag-of-words: the multiset of tokens, order discarded.

```text
d1 tokens: ['the', 'pump', 'failed']
d1 vector: [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
```

Do it for all four documents and you have the [document-term matrix]{.hl},
the central object of classical NLP. Rows are documents, columns are words:

```text
          d1  d2  d3  d4
failed     1   0   1   0
leak       0   0   0   1
pump       1   1   0   0
repaired   0   0   0   1
replaced   0   1   0   0
seal       0   0   0   1
the        1   1   1   1
valve      0   0   1   0
was        0   1   0   1
```

**Note the orientation.** In the standard layout rows are documents and
columns are terms; here the matrix is 4 documents × 9 terms. The block above is
only shown transposed so that it fits the page.

::: {#gloss-feature .column-margin .term-gloss}
**feature** — one measured column of your data. Here, one word. If you
come from statistics, this is simply a predictor variable under a
different name. [↩](#term-feature){.term-back}
:::

A statistician should recognize this immediately: it is a design matrix.
Each document is an observation, each word is a [feature](#gloss-feature){#term-feature .term-ref}, and everything you
know about regression with many correlated, mostly-zero predictors now
applies.

### Step 4 — does every word deserve the same weight?

We have numbers now. The question nobody asks early enough is whether they
are the *right* numbers.

Look at the row for `the`. It appears in all four documents, so it
contributes to every comparison while distinguishing nothing. Meanwhile
`valve` appears once and is the only thing that makes d3 distinctive. Raw
counts give them the same treatment.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Two questions before the formula.** To give a term a high weight we want two
things:

1. **It is frequent in this document.** The factor that measures this is
   **TF**.
2. **It is not ordinary across all documents.** The factor that measures this
   is **IDF**.

TF-IDF is the product of the answers. The formulas below are one particular way
of turning those two questions into numbers.
:::

We want a weight that is high when a word is frequent *in this document*
and rare *across documents*. Splitting that into two factors gives TF-IDF.

**Term frequency** is how often the word occurs in this document — the *raw*
count we already have. Note *raw*: `scikit-learn` does not divide by document
length here, because the L2 normalization in step 5 handles length.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Practice note: TF-IDF is not one formula

Many textbooks define term frequency as $\mathrm{tf} = c(t,d)/|d|$, or as the
logarithmic $1 + \log c(t,d)$, and the resulting numbers differ. The classical
shorthand for naming a variant is SMART notation, a three-letter code for
(tf) × (idf) × (normalization): `scikit-learn`'s default is roughly **`ntc`** —
natural tf, smoothed idf, cosine normalization — where a common classic IR
choice is **`ltc`**, with logarithmic tf. Setting `sublinear_tf=True` moves you from
`n` to `l`, and it is the option that wins a row in the experiment at the end
of this chapter. Say which variant produced a number you report; "TF-IDF" on
its own is not a specification.
:::

::: {#gloss-document-frequency-df .column-margin .term-gloss}
**document frequency (df)** — in how many documents a word shows up at
all, no matter how often it shows up in each. A word in every document
tells you nothing about any of them. [↩](#term-document-frequency-df){.term-back}
:::

**[Document frequency](#gloss-document-frequency-df){#term-document-frequency-df .term-ref}**, $\mathrm{df}(t)$, is how many documents contain the
word at all. We want the weight to fall as df rises, so we invert it. But raw
inversion, $1/\mathrm{df}$, is too aggressive, because its range is far too
wide. In a collection of a thousand documents, a term in one document gets
$1/\mathrm{df} = 1$ and a term in every document gets $0.001$: a thousandfold
gap. A handful of rare terms — often typos and one-off names — would soak up
nearly all the weight and swamp everything else. A logarithm compresses that
range: $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ stays between $\ln 1000 \approx 6.9$ and 0 in the
same collection, and doubling the document frequency costs the same amount
($\ln 2 \approx 0.69$) wherever it happens. The second justification comes
from information theory: $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ is the self-information of
seeing the term in a document (see the intuition check below)
[@sparckjones1972statistical]. The basic form is:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)}\right)
$$

Libraries adjust that basic form a little, because $\mathrm{df}$ can be zero
and because you rarely want a term that appears in every document to fall to
exactly zero weight. The smoothed form `scikit-learn` uses is:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1 + n}{1 + \mathrm{df}(t)}\right) + 1
$$

Read the formula one symbol at a time. $t$ is a term, $n$ is the number of
documents in the collection, and $\mathrm{df}(t)$ counts how many of them
contain $t$ at least once. The $1+$ terms are smoothing, and they
have a clean reading: the formula behaves exactly as if the collection held one
**extra document containing every term once**. That imaginary document is why
$\mathrm{df}$ can never be zero and why no weight can run away, and it is the
same add-one idea you will meet again as Laplace smoothing in
@sec-language-models. The trailing $+1$ then guarantees that a word appearing
everywhere still gets a weight of 1 rather than 0, so it is down-weighted
rather than deleted. This is `scikit-learn`'s exact formula;
other libraries differ in the details, which is a classic source of "why
don't my numbers match".

**Work two of them by hand.** Our corpus has $n = 4$ documents. The word
`pump` appears in d1 and d2, so $\mathrm{df} = 2$:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(\texttt{pump}) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1+4}{1+2}\right) + 1
= \ln(1.667) + 1 = 0.511 + 1 = 1.511
$$

The word `the` appears in all four, so $\mathrm{df} = 4$:

$$
\mathrm{idf}(\texttt{the}) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1+4}{1+4}\right) + 1
= \ln(1) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1
$$

That second line is the whole design in miniature. A word that is everywhere
tells you nothing about *which* document you are holding, so the ratio inside
the log collapses to 1, the log collapses to 0, and the term is left standing
on the floor weight of 1. It is not deleted — it is told that it gets one
vote while `pump` gets one and a half.

::: {.column-margin}
The librarian's version. Ask for "the book about pumps" and the word *the*
narrows the shelf down not at all, while *pumps* narrows it to a metre of
shelving. IDF is a number for how much a word narrows the search.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Intuition check: why the logarithm?

This is one of the most common interview questions in the whole field, and
the weak answer is "to prevent the weight from getting too big."

The better answer has two parts.

**It compresses the range.** Informativeness is not linear in rarity, but that
alone does not call for a logarithm: $1/\mathrm{df}$ is also a decreasing,
flattening curve. The difference is the range. In a collection of 10,000
documents, $1/\mathrm{df}$ puts a ten-thousandfold gap between a term in one
document and a term in every document, and a few rare terms take over every
similarity. $\log(n/\mathrm{df})$ stays between 9.2 and 0 and treats equal
ratios equally: raising df from 1 to 10 costs the same weight
($\ln 10 \approx 2.3$) as raising it from 1,000 to 10,000.

**It is a probability in disguise.** If $\mathrm{df}(t)/n$ estimates the
probability that a random document contains $t$, then
$\log \frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} = -\log P(t)$ — the *self-information* of
seeing that term, in the information-theoretic sense. Rare events carry more
information, and the log is not a trick for making numbers smaller; it is what
information *is*. Robertson's paper [@robertson2004understanding] is the
careful treatment, and the honest history is that Spärck Jones proposed IDF
on empirical grounds in 1972 and the theory was reverse-engineered later.

**And Zipf closes the loop.** As you saw earlier in this chapter, word
frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank: a handful of words have
enormous counts and tens of thousands have tiny ones. On a scale that skewed,
raw differences mislead — the log measures a difference as a *ratio* rather
than a count, and straightens the distribution into a line. It is the same
reason you log-transform income or city size: there too a few giants flatten
everyone else off the scale.
:::

Here are the document frequencies and IDF values for our corpus, computed by
hand and then checked against the library:

```python
import numpy as np

n = len(corpus)
df = (X.toarray() > 0).sum(axis=0)
idf_manual = np.log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1
```

```text
          df     idf
failed     2  1.5108
leak       1  1.9163
pump       2  1.5108
repaired   1  1.9163
replaced   1  1.9163
seal       1  1.9163
the        4  1.0000
valve      1  1.9163
was        2  1.5108

sklearn idf_: [1.5108 1.9163 1.5108 1.9163 1.9163 1.9163 1. 1.9163 1.5108]
max abs diff vs manual: 0.0
```

`the` is in all four documents and lands exactly on the floor of 1.0. Every
word unique to one document gets 1.9163. The ordering is the point: the
weight is a monotone decreasing function of how many documents a word
appears in.

On the real corpus the spread is much larger:

```text
the            df=  9477  df/N= 0.838  idf= 1.18
is             df=  7034  df/N= 0.622  idf= 1.48
car            df=   394  df/N= 0.035  idf= 4.35
encryption     df=   169  df/N= 0.015  idf= 5.20
gravitational  df=     8  df/N= 0.001  idf= 8.14
```

### Step 5 — multiply, then normalize

Two ingredients are on the table: a count that says how often a word appears
*here*, and a weight that says how unusual it is *everywhere*. Combining them
is the last piece of arithmetic in this chapter, and it is a multiplication
followed by a division.

Before the mathematics, the reason for that division, as a question: why should
two documents on the same topic — one 20 words long, the other 2,000 — look far
apart only because one is longer? Every count in the long document is bigger, so
its vector is longer. L2 normalization removes exactly that length effect and
leaves behind how the document distributes its weight across terms.

::: {#gloss-tf-idf .column-margin .term-gloss}
**TF-IDF** — score each word in a document by how often it appears here, and
reduce that score as the word becomes more widespread across the collection.
Frequent-and-rare wins; frequent-and-everywhere loses. [↩](#term-tf-idf){.term-back}
:::

[TF-IDF](#gloss-tf-idf){#term-tf-idf .term-ref} is the product, computed cell by cell. For d1 (`the pump failed`):

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

counts = X.toarray()[0]
weighted = counts * idf_manual
norm = np.linalg.norm(weighted)
print("counts        :", counts)
print("times idf     :", weighted.round(4))
print("l2 norm       :", round(norm, 4))
print("normalized    :", (weighted / norm).round(4))
print("sklearn row d1:", TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus).toarray()[0].round(4))
```

```text
counts        : [1 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0]
times idf     : [1.5108 0.     1.5108 0.     0.     0.     1.     0.     0.    ]
l2 norm       : 2.3591
normalized    : [0.6404 0.     0.6404 0.     0.     0.     0.4239 0.     0.    ]
sklearn row d1: [0.6404 0.     0.6404 0.     0.     0.     0.4239 0.     0.    ]
```

That last pair of lines is the point of this whole section: the hand
computation and `TfidfVectorizer` agree to every digit. There is no magic in
the library.

Follow one row all the way through. d1 is `the pump failed`, so three
positions are non-zero, each with a count of 1. Multiply each by its IDF and
you get $1.5108$ for `failed`, $1.5108$ for `pump`, and $1.0000$ for `the`.
The length of that vector is the ordinary Pythagorean one, extended to nine
dimensions — square, add, take the root:

$$
\lVert v \rVert_2 = \sqrt{1.5108^2 + 1.5108^2 + 1.0000^2}
\approx \sqrt{2.28259 + 2.28259 + 1.00000} = \sqrt{5.56518} \approx 2.3591
$$

Intermediate values are rounded for display; carried at full precision the norm
is $2.35906509\ldots$, which is what the library uses.

The six zero entries contribute nothing, which is why this stays cheap even
when the vocabulary has 200,000 columns. Divide through:

$$
\frac{1.5108}{2.3591} = 0.6404
\qquad
\frac{1.0000}{2.3591} = 0.4239
$$

and those are exactly the numbers `TfidfVectorizer` printed above.

That final division by $\lVert v \rVert_2$ is [L2 normalization]{.hl}, and it
is not cosmetic. Without it, a long document has a large vector simply for
being long, and every comparison based on a dot product or Euclidean distance
— including a linear classifier's score — becomes partly a comparison of
document lengths. (Cosine divides by the norms itself, so it is immune; see
below.) Normalizing puts every document on the unit sphere, so only
*direction* — the mix of words — carries information.

The particular combination you have just built — term frequency, times
inverse document frequency, then length-normalized — is not the only one
anyone tried. Salton and Buckley [@salton1988term] compared a large family of
weighting schemes empirically and this is roughly the one that won, which is
why it became the default in every library you will touch.

::: {.column-margin}
Think of it as putting every document on a sphere of the same radius. A 50-word
report and a 5,000-word report both end up at unit *length* — the squares of
the components sum to one, not the components themselves — so the question
becomes which direction each one points, not how far it reaches.

One document cannot be put on the sphere: an empty one, or one whose every
word is out of vocabulary, has $\lVert v \rVert_2 = 0$ and no direction to
normalize. Cosine with it is $0/0$ — undefined. `scikit-learn` returns a zero
row and a cosine of 0, which is a convention rather than an answer; if such
documents exist in your corpus, count them before you trust any similarity
built on them.
:::

### Step 6 — comparing documents with cosine similarity

Every document is now a point in $\mathbb{R}^9$. Which finally lets us ask
the question the whole chapter has been building towards: are these two
documents about the same thing?

::: {#gloss-cosine-similarity .column-margin .term-gloss}
**cosine similarity** — how closely two documents point in the same
direction, ignoring how long they are. It is why a two-line note and a
ten-page report can still count as being about the same thing. [↩](#term-cosine-similarity){.term-back}
:::

The sentence to keep: **cosine similarity compares direction, not length.**
Two normalized vectors are compared by their dot product, which is the
cosine of the angle between them. That number is their [cosine similarity](#gloss-cosine-similarity){#term-cosine-similarity .term-ref}:
1 means identical direction, 0 means no shared vocabulary. The equivalence with
Euclidean distance in the box below is a detail on top of that intuition, not a
replacement for it.

$$
\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}
= \sum_{i} a_i b_i \quad \text{(when both are already unit length)}
$$

**Compute one cell by hand.** d1 is `the pump failed` and d3 is
`the valve failed`; they share `failed` and `the` and disagree everywhere
else. Only positions where *both* vectors are non-zero can contribute, so the
whole nine-dimensional sum has exactly two live terms:

$$
\cos(\text{d1}, \text{d3}) =
\underbrace{0.6404 \times 0.5729}_{\texttt{failed}} +
\underbrace{0.4239 \times 0.3792}_{\texttt{the}}
= 0.3669 + 0.1607 = 0.528
$$

Notice how uneven that is. `failed` supplies 70% of the similarity and
`the` supplies 30%, even though each word occurs exactly once in each
document. Under raw counts they would have contributed equally. [The
weighting is what decides which shared word counts as evidence.]{.hl}

```python
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

T = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)   # the TF-IDF rows from step 5
print(cosine_similarity(T).round(3))          # top panel
print(cosine_similarity(X).round(3))          # bottom panel: raw counts from step 1
```

Row and column labels were added to the output for readability:

```text
       d1     d2     d3     d4          <- TF-IDF
d1  1.000  0.458  0.528  0.112
d2  0.458  1.000  0.125  0.286
d3  0.528  0.125  1.000  0.100
d4  0.112  0.286  0.100  1.000

       d1     d2     d3     d4          <- raw counts
d1  1.000  0.577  0.667  0.258
d2  0.577  1.000  0.289  0.447
d3  0.667  0.289  1.000  0.258
d4  0.258  0.447  0.258  1.000
```

Compare the two panels. Under raw counts, d1 and d4 sit at a cosine of 0.26 —
but they share only the word `the`. TF-IDF correctly pulls that down to 0.11.
(A cosine is the cosine of the angle between the two vectors. It is not a
calibrated percentage of semantic similarity, which is what reporting it as
"26% similar" implies.)
Every pair drops, and the pairs that drop most are the ones whose only
common ground was a stop word.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Why cosine and not Euclidean distance</div>
```
